content: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. {{v:2}} The same was in the beginning with God. {{v:3}} All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made. {{v:4}} In him was life, and the life was the light of men. {{v:5}} The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.

facets.evidence: Intertextual echo of Gen 1:1 ('In the beginning') is the evident sense recognized universally in patristic and modern commentary; the identification of the Word as pre-temporal follows directly from 'In the beginning was the Word' — 'was' places him before the beginning, not within it.
facets.text: The Prologue opens with the same words as Genesis, "In the beginning," deliberately echoing the first creation to announce a new one. By naming the Word (Logos) as already existing "in the beginning," John locates Christ before all created time, identifying him not as the first of creatures but as the eternal one through whom creation itself begins.
facets.question: Why does John's Gospel begin with the same words as Genesis?

facets.evidence: Plain-sense tension between 'the Word was with God' (distinction of persons) and 'the Word was God' (identity of divine nature) is the classical Trinitarian proof-text; patristic consensus (e.g., Athanasius, Augustine) and CCC 240–241 read these clauses as guarding against Arianism and Sabellianism, making the Trinitarian reading a settled one-step inference.
facets.text: In three clauses John holds together the Word's distinct personhood and full divinity: the Word was "with God," preserving the real relation between Father and Son, yet the Word "was God," affirming that he is not a lesser being but shares the one divine nature. This verse is a scriptural foundation for the doctrine of the Trinity, guarding against both confusing the persons and dividing the substance.
facets.question: How can the Word be both with God and be God?

facets.evidence: All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made.
facets.text: The Word is the agent of all creation: "All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made." This teaches that nothing in existence stands apart from the Son, so that the same one who redeems the world is the one through whom the world was first spoken into being, uniting creation and redemption in a single divine Word.
facets.question: What role does the Word have in the creation of everything?

facets.evidence: Evident arc of the verse: 'In him was life, and the life was the light of men' identifies the Word as the originating source of both life and light for humanity; the further step that 'light' denotes divine truth and holiness and that illumination is participation in the Word's own life is a one-step reading secured by Johannine usage throughout the Gospel (e.g., John 8:12, 14:6) and patristic tradition.
facets.text: "In him was life, and the life was the light of men" presents Christ not merely as a teacher who gives light but as the very source of life and illumination for humanity. The image of light points to divine truth, holiness, and the knowledge of God, so that to be enlightened is to be drawn into the life of the Word himself.
facets.question: What does it mean that the Word is the life and light of humanity?

facets.evidence: The passage states the light shines and darkness has not overcome it, but the identification of 'darkness' specifically with sin, ignorance, and death, and the anticipation of Cross and Resurrection as the decisive conquest, requires connecting this verse to the broader Johannine theology and Gospel narrative — an argument a theologian would defend but the text does not state.
facets.text: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn't overcome it" sounds the note of victory that governs the whole Gospel: the darkness of sin, ignorance, and death cannot extinguish or comprehend the divine light. Written in the present tense, it declares an ongoing reality, anticipating the Cross and Resurrection where the light decisively conquers.
facets.question: What is meant by the darkness not overcoming the light?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: John 1:1–5, the Johannine Prologue, introduces the eternal Logos (Word) as the divine agent of creation, the source of life and light for humanity, and the conquering light that darkness cannot overcome — establishing foundational doctrines of the Trinity, the pre-existence of Christ, and the unity of creation and redemption.

[scriptural/doctrinal | settled]: The deliberate echo of Genesis 1:1 in John's opening phrase signals that the Evangelist is announcing a new creation narrative, while the eternal pre-existence of the Logos places Christ outside and before created time — not as the highest creature but as the uncreated one through whom all things come to be.

[doctrinal/scriptural | settled]: The three ascending clauses of John 1:1 — the Word with God, and the Word being God — provide a primary scriptural warrant for Trinitarian theology, affirming both the distinct personal relationship of the Son to the Father and the complete sharing of a single divine nature, thereby guarding against both modalism and subordinationism.

[doctrinal/scriptural | explicit]: As the mediator of all creation, the Son is the one through whom every existing thing was brought into being, leaving nothing outside his authorship; this inseparable bond between the creative and redemptive work of the same eternal Word unifies cosmology and soteriology in Johannine theology.

[doctrinal/devotional | settled]: Christ is identified not as a mere revealer or enlightened teacher but as the ontological source of life itself and of genuine illumination for the human race; to receive the light of the Logos is to be drawn into participation in divine life, truth, and the knowledge of God — a theme central to Johannine spirituality and mystical theology.

[scriptural/doctrinal | inferential]: The present-tense declaration that the light shines and the darkness has not prevailed against it frames the entire Fourth Gospel as a testimony to ongoing divine victory; the darkness — encompassing sin, spiritual blindness, and death — is powerless to extinguish the divine light, a claim that proleptically anticipates the triumph of the Cross and Resurrection.
